title: Medicare-First Longevity Kit for Independent Practices
one_liner: Longevity medicine built on what Medicare already pays for, sold as a workflow kit to independent primary-care practices.
customer: Independent primary-care and DPC-adjacent practices (2-15 clinicians) with 500-2,000 Medicare patients each.
problem: The longevity boom (Function $2.5B, Neko ~$7B, Superpower up to $349/yr) targets cash-paying under-55s, while the highest-risk group, seniors, has a covered prevention stack that is badly under-used. Well under half of beneficiaries take the Annual Wellness Visit, and independents lack the workflow to turn covered services into a healthspan program.
solution: A configurable 'healthspan AWV' template with functional tests (chair-stand, grip, gait speed), cognitive and falls screens, covered lipid, diabetes and bone screening, and vaccine gap-closing. A monthly care-management billing layer (APCM codes introduced in 2025). Compliant ABN-based cash upsells for ApoB or Lp(a). Practices get scripts, patient handouts and a collections dashboard.
why_now: APCM monthly primary-care codes are new (2025). The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge began Jul 1, 2026, pulling seniors into metabolic care. Cash longevity prices keep rising, which cedes the 65+ segment. About 82% of doctors are employed, so the remaining independents are underserved by digital vendors.
revenue_model: $600-1,200/month SaaS per practice plus 15-20% of incremental collected revenue (est. $30-80k per clinician per year of newly captured billing).
non_obvious_insight: 'Longevity' for the 65+ is mostly a billing-and-workflow problem on already-covered benefits. Founders build for cash because that is where the venture buzz is, and they overlook the biggest and sickest demographic, whose payer is already at the table.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 independent practices via state IPAs and DPC-Medicare communities. Offer a free 30-day audit of their AWV and care-management capture, pulled from claims, showing dollars left on the table. Convert to a $499/month pilot with a success fee.

title: Ceremony-as-a-Service for Direct Cremation Providers
one_liner: White-label the memorial gathering that low-cost cremation providers can't deliver, so families buy a $1.5K box of ashes plus a $3.5K send-off.
customer: Direct-cremation companies (online and storefront), hospices and community organizations. Families pay for the events.
problem: NFDA projects cremation at 63.4% in 2025, rising to 82.3% by 2045. Direct-cremation providers win on price but hand families ashes with no ceremony. Consolidators' chapels and $8K packages don't fit that customer. NFDA reports 58.3% of consumers have attended services at unconventional venues, so demand exists but no one owns the coordination.
solution: A 'Celebration Desk' embedded in the provider's checkout as 'add a gathering'. A coordinator plus software books non-funeral venues (breweries, restaurants, parks, boats, halls), catering, a celebrant, a slideshow, live-stream and RSVPs. Packages are fixed-price at $1,500, $3,500 or $7,500. It also handles scattering permits and follow-up.
why_now: Direct cremation share keeps climbing. NFDA says 61.4% of consumers are interested in green options. Consolidators are structurally pinned to a 58% cremation mix and 3%+ annual price increases and cannot copy an unbundled model. Venues have empty weekday capacity and live-streaming is now trivial.
revenue_model: Fixed package fee at 35-45% gross margin, 10-15% rev share from venues and caterers, and a referral or white-label fee of $150-$300 per booked event to the cremation provider.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders see direct cremation as the industry's price-war threat. It is really an unbundling that turned the ceremony into a separate, high-margin purchase that nobody owns. The providers who created it have no event staff, and the consolidators' chapels are the wrong shape.
first_30_days: Pick one metro. Sign one direct-cremation provider and ten venues. Coordinate the first five events by hand at about $1,800 each, offered through the provider's post-arrangement email. Photograph and price each event to build the package catalog.

title: Phishing Simulations for Agent Approvers
one_liner: Plant known-bad agent actions into human approval queues and prove to auditors and insurers that your reviewers actually catch them.
customer: Heads of finance ops, claims, compliance and internal audit at companies whose agents require human approval (payments, refunds, claims, access requests, code merges), plus cyber underwriters who ask about controls.
problem: Human-in-the-loop is the default answer to agent risk. Step two: volume makes approval a reflex, so the gate decays into a rubber stamp. Step three: regulators and auditors ask for oversight that is demonstrable and measurable (EU AI Act Article 14 and NIST AI RMF language), and no company can show that reviewers catch anything. Injected test cases are recommended in practice writing, but nobody productizes them.
solution: Middleware in the approval path (Slack, Teams, ServiceNow or custom queues) that injects synthetic, internally labeled bad cases at calibrated rates: a vendor bank-detail change, an out-of-policy refund, a prompt-injected request. It measures catch rate and latency by reviewer, queue and time of day, and adapts injection frequency. Output is an oversight effectiveness report with confidence intervals for auditors and insurers, plus queue-design advice (fewer, better gates).
why_now: Agents multiply approval volume. The EU AI Act's human-oversight requirements are still on the books for 2027 and insurers now ask about controls in questionnaires. Approval fatigue is widely acknowledged but unmeasured.
revenue_model: $2-8k/month per approval workflow, or $30-$100k/year enterprise licenses, with an audit-evidence add-on.
non_obvious_insight: KnowBe4 built a large company by testing humans rather than training them. The presence of a reviewer is not a control, but a measured catch rate is, and it doubles as evidence in insurance and audit conversations.
first_30_days: Build for Slack approvals with an accounts-payable bank-change scenario. Run it with 3 finance-ops teams and deliver a first report stating how many planted errors reviewers caught. Use anonymized catch-rate results as the sales asset.

title: Beaver Warranty for County Culverts and Roads
one_liner: A 5-year no-clog guarantee that keeps beavers out of culverts using flow devices and sensors, and later sells the wetlands they build to water and wildfire agencies.
customer: County and municipal public works departments, state DOTs and railroads, and later water utilities and wildfire agencies.
problem: Beavers plug culverts, flooding roads and forcing repeated trapping, dam breaching and clearing, which costs taxpayers every year and never ends because new beavers arrive. Managers have no reliable, maintenance-free alternative and little data on true costs.
solution: A fixed-price warranty that installs proven flow devices (culvert fences and pond levelers), adds low-cost water-level sensors and cameras, and covers every follow-up visit. Evidence in hand: Virginia's DOT spent more than $300,000 a year on prevention, repairs and removal before devices, versus under $45,000 for installation and $277 a year to maintain; and Billerica, MA found trapping and breaching cost $409 per site per year versus $229 for devices. Well-designed culvert fences reportedly succeed 95% of the time. Once the culvert is solved, we offer beaver dam analogs and habitat as water storage and fire refuge.
why_now: California's Beaver Restoration Program (2023) had received 26 proposals by April 2026, and CDFW grants have funded over 100 beaver dam analogs. Wildfire and drought budgets are looking for nature-based solutions. Cheap IoT level sensors make a guarantee affordable to price and monitor.
revenue_model: Installs of roughly $8-45k per site or bundle, an annual monitoring and warranty fee of $300-1,000, and later performance contracts with water and fire agencies for stored water or refuge acres.
non_obvious_insight: The county does not pay to deal with beavers, it pays for recurring emergency labor, so sell an insurance-style warranty backed by data, not a wildlife product. After the culvert is fixed, the beaver becomes a free crew building water storage that a different agency will pay for, so the same animal is a liability line item for one customer and an asset for another.
first_30_days: File public-records requests in five counties for trapping and culvert-clearing spend. Offer to fix the three worst culverts at cost in exchange for cost data and a case study, then sell sub-$50k warranties that fit under small-purchase thresholds.

title: Fall Response Network for Meteorite Hunters
one_liner: Rapid strewn-field prediction plus standard landowner-permission contracts and a fresh-fall sales channel for meteorite hunters, extendable to satellite-debris reentries.
customer: Serious hunters and dealers (subscription), landowners and park districts (permission desks), and buyers of fresh-fall specimens.
problem: The 17 March 2026 Ohio fall drew swarms of hunters, with pieces going for roughly $400-500 per gram early on, while a golf club closed its property and a park district warned hunters off. Permission takes days, fresh-fall value decays fast, and there is no standard revenue share with landowners.
solution: Alerts within 30-60 minutes combining public bolide and radar data with hobby camera networks and automated strewn maps. A pre-registered hunter roster with waivers, a standard landowner-share contract signed digitally, on-site chain of custody, classification via a partner lab, and consignment to dealers and museums.
why_now: The Ohio fall made the economics and the access conflict public. Open satellite and radar data and cheap all-sky cameras exist, and Starlink reentries add a second, insurer-relevant use case.
revenue_model: $20/month alerts, 10-15% of specimen sales, landowner-desk fees from park districts and insurers, and data licensing.
non_obvious_insight: Strewn-field maps are already published free, so the scarce thing is access and legitimacy in the first 72 hours. A contract-and-permission layer turns hostile landowners into revenue partners and creates an exclusive right-of-entry that cannot be scraped.
first_30_days: Build a 200-person hunter Discord and draft a standard landowner agreement. Test it on the next reported fireball with 20 landowners, and sign 2 dealers to buy through the network.

title: Standby Mass-Fatality Cooler Network for Counties
one_liner: A retainer-based network of vetted funeral homes with cooler space, vans and chain-of-custody training that counties and hospital coalitions can activate when the morgue overflows.
customer: County emergency managers, medical examiner and coroner offices, regional Health Care Coalitions and hospital systems. They fund it through preparedness grants, state emergency-management budgets and hospital readiness budgets.
problem: Mass-fatality plans routinely say 'coordinate with local funeral directors', which is a handshake with no contract, no capacity inventory, no shared identification protocol and no payment. ME planning guides size storage at roughly 1.5x average daily caseload plus a 25% surge buffer, so a heat wave, hurricane, flood or outbreak blows through it. Counties then scramble for refrigerated trailers, which are undignified, poorly tracked, and a magnet for misidentification scandals. Funeral homes are willing to help but can't say what they can commit and dread not being paid.
solution: Enroll 10-30 funeral homes per region. Run a capacity survey (cooler slots, bariatric capability, generators, on-call staff, vehicles). Train them in ID and chain-of-custody basics, personal-effects logging and family-notification etiquette, a DMORT-lite curriculum. Credential their licenses and insurance. Provide a shared dashboard and case-tracking app with unique IDs, tags, photos and effects logs that exports to the ME's systems. Sell the county or coalition a one-to-three-year readiness retainer with an annual tabletop exercise and pre-negotiated per-diem activation rates. Add an 'everyday overflow' service for ME backlogs, such as holiday weekends and opioid or heat spikes, at per-case rates, which turns readiness into recurring revenue.
why_now: Federal disaster support is being pushed toward states and counties, so local preparedness is becoming a locally funded line item. Record heat deaths in the Southwest and busy hurricane seasons keep overloading morgues. ME offices are visibly overflowing, and new facilities such as Jacksonville's in 2026 are being built with triple capacity. Forensic pathologist shortages slow releases and keep bodies in coolers longer.
revenue_model: Annual readiness retainer of $15,000-$60,000 per county or coalition region, with a stipend of about $3,000-$8,000 flowing to each participating funeral home. Activation per diem of $75-$150 per body per day. Overflow per-case fees. $8,000-$15,000 for tabletop exercises and training. Software license for the tracking app.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset in a mass-fatality event isn't refrigerated trucks, it's trusted, licensed humans with cooled rooms already in every zip code, and they sit about 70% idle. No one has ever paid funeral homes to stay ready. Public trust collapses over identification and chain-of-custody errors, not storage, and funeral directors are the only civilians who do that work every day.
first_30_days: Pick one heat- and hurricane-exposed region. Recruit 10-15 funeral homes through the state funeral directors' association. Write a 12-page letter-of-commitment and capacity template. Book meetings with five county emergency managers and two Health Care Coalition coordinators (public directories). Offer a $7,500 paid tabletop exercise plus regional capacity map, priced under many small-purchase thresholds. Convert the exercise participants to a retainer proposal.

title: Universal Insurance Claims Rails for Vet Front Desks
one_liner: Vet front desks lose hours filing claims in a dozen insurer portals; sell them one submission and status layer, then add pre-approval and instant-pay as insurers plug in.
customer: Independent clinics and small groups (1-20 locations) with 15-30% insured patients. Later, insurers as per-claim payers.
problem: There are about 6.98M insured animals (+9% in 2025), each insurer has its own portal, forms and record requests, and only 48.2% of practices proactively recommend insurance. Owners often front the full bill. Insurers cannot see clinics, so they lack pre-authorization, real-time pricing and fraud tools.
solution: A browser agent inside the PIMS invoice screen, later API-connected, sends invoice plus records to the right insurer by policy number, tracks status, chases missing documents and reconciles payments. Once volume gives risk data, offer a direct-pay advance so the owner only pays the deductible at checkout.
why_now: Insured animals keep growing while premiums outpace enrollment, so insurers want lower cost-to-adjudicate. Computer-use LLM agents can operate portals without waiting for API deals. Ambient scribes are producing more structured records for claims.
revenue_model: $99-199 per clinic per month, $1-3 per clean claim from insurers later, and a 2-3% fee on advanced claims.
non_obvious_insight: Insurance penetration is partly a back-office problem: the clinic is the distribution channel and is punished with admin work for recommending coverage. Remove the penalty and the recommendation rate rises. The clearinghouse owns the claims data insurers currently cannot see.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 clinics through cloud-PIMS user groups. Shadow the front desk for a week and automate the top 5 insurers by portal. Offer 30 days free, then $99 per month. Measure hours saved per week and days-to-payment.

title: Evac Cash: Payout When Ordered to Evacuate
one_liner: A few dollars a month buys a $500-$2,500 wire within hours of an official mandatory evacuation order for your address, covering hurricane, wildfire and burn-scar flood orders.
customer: Renters and lower-to-middle-income homeowners in evacuation zones: Gulf and Florida surge zones, Western wildfire-urban-interface neighborhoods, and LA burn-scar areas. Sold to individuals, through employers of hourly staff (hospitals, hotels, nursing homes, grocers), and through credit unions or municipal 'evac funds'.
problem: Evacuating costs $1,000-$3,000 (gas, hotel, lost shifts, pet boarding) and the money is needed before any claim exists. Cost is a common reason people stay, so the people most exposed are least able to leave. Civil-authority and additional-living-expense cover is slow, receipt-based, often conditional on nearby damage, and many renters lack it.
solution: A parametric contract whose trigger is a legal act. If your geocoded address sits inside a polygon under a mandatory evacuation order, or an NWS flash-flood emergency for a burn scar, the platform pays via FedNow/RTP or a push-to-card within hours. Zone data comes from county emergency-management systems (evacuation-zone platforms and state zone maps). Tiers are priced by zone frequency, with one payout per event per address and a simple app that alerts you and shows your zone. Underwritten via a licensed MGA and fronting carrier, first as employer group policies.
why_now: Address-level, machine-readable evacuation zones are now common. FedNow/RTP make hours-not-weeks payouts cheap. The LA fires of January 2025 made burn-scar exposure vivid, and NOAA CPC/IRI's September 2026 outlooks show a greater than 90% chance of a very strong El Niño this winter, which means heavy rain on fresh burn scars and flash-flood/debris-flow evacuation orders. Parametric reinsurance capacity is plentiful and MGAs want small-ticket distribution.
revenue_model: Premium of roughly $3-$15 per month depending on how often each zone is ordered out (about 1.3-1.5x expected payout), or $1-$3 per employee per month on group plans. The company keeps an MGA commission of 15-25%, plus municipal, nonprofit and employer-funded policies for vulnerable residents. Later it can sell zone-frequency data to emergency managers.
non_obvious_insight: The best parametric trigger is a legal act, not a physical measurement. An evacuation order is binary, public, address-specific and timestamped, so basis risk nearly vanishes. Paying people to leave also changes behavior and saves lives, which makes employers and governments willing co-payers, so the product has two buyers instead of one.
first_30_days: Sign a parametric MGA and fronting carrier. Build the polygon match and instant-payout flow on public evacuation-zone data. Pilot a group policy for about 200 hourly workers at one Gulf hospital or hotel employer and one credit union serving a LA burn-scar community. Offer emergency-management agencies a free 'what zone am I in' tool for distribution. Goal: 500 covered addresses before peak rain season.

title: Contingency-Fee Meter Audits for Water Utilities
one_liner: Test the big commercial and industrial meters that under-register, replace them, and take a share of the new billed revenue for two years.
customer: Mid-size water and wastewater utilities (20k-500k connections) with large commercial bases, private regulated water companies, and utilities serving new large loads such as data centers and fabs. The utility pays from recovered revenue.
problem: Everyone sells AI leak detection, but in many audits apparent losses (meter under-registration, billing errors, unauthorized use) are comparable to real losses. Large compound meters under-register at low flow, and 1% of a data center's consumption is a lot of money. Utilities under rate pressure and drought-reduced volumes have no capex budget for meter programs.
solution: Prioritize the top 5% of accounts using billing anomalies (size versus consumption history). Field-test meters with a mobile test bench and clamp-on verification, then repair or replace. The company fronts the work and takes 20-35% of incremental revenue for 24 months. Software ranks accounts, and reports feed the AWWA-style utility audit.
why_now: Drought cuts volumes and rate pressure is intense. Private water companies invested about $6.8B in 2025 and must justify revenue. New industrial loads make each meter worth more.
revenue_model: 20-35% of incremental billed revenue for two years, with no upfront cost to the utility.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders chase leaks, which need capital and crews. Meter recovery is immediate cash with no capex approval, so it is easy to say yes to. Private and special-district utilities can sign contingency deals without a full municipal procurement.
first_30_days: Target three investor-owned utilities and two special districts. Offer a free desktop analysis of their top 200 commercial accounts using billing data. Test the ten most suspicious meters as a proof-of-value, and sign a contingency contract on the results.

title: Inheriting the Lease: Rent-Stabilized Succession Service
one_liner: A service that helps families of rent-regulated elders build and keep the co-residency evidence that lets them inherit a below-market lease, and files the succession claim within days of a death.
customer: Adult children and relatives living with rent-stabilized or rent-controlled elders (about 1M stabilized units in NYC alone, plus SF, LA, Newark and DC). Elder-law and tenant-rights attorneys, senior centers, home-care agencies and hospital discharge planners white-label or refer.
problem: In regulated housing, a family member who can prove co-residency (typically 2 years, or 1 for seniors and the disabled) can succeed to the lease. The lease can be worth six figures over time. Landlords, who gain by re-renting at market, often contest, and the outcome hinges on documents families never assembled while the elder was alive (IDs, tax returns, bills, benefit and medical mail). After death the family faces a notice in weeks, with the elder's records locked in an unopened estate.
solution: Run a lease-inheritance readiness audit and an evidence ledger that collects only genuine documents (address-bearing IDs, filings, bank and medical mail, affidavits from neighbors). After a death, generate a Day-1 succession packet: notice to the landlord, agency filings, and attorney referral. Contested cases go to partner lawyers on contingency or through right-to-counsel programs.
why_now: NYC's political shift toward tenant protection, the SF rent emergency and record middle-income rent distress raise the stakes. The first Boomer tenants are aging out. Good Cause protections and local rent laws expand the leases worth inheriting. AI-generated pleadings are flooding housing courts, which raises the value of clean, verifiable evidence.
revenue_model: $199-399 per family file plus $6-9 per month for the evidence ledger. White-label and per-file fees from law firms, nonprofits and home-care agencies. Referral fees from partner attorneys.
non_obvious_insight: For many urban middle-class families the biggest asset passed at death is not money but a below-market lease, and the value is lost through missing paperwork, not through the law. The $124T wealth-transfer statistics ignore it entirely.
first_30_days: With two elder-law attorneys, draft evidence checklists from the state rent-stabilization rules. Run three clinics at senior centers or tenant associations. Charge $199 for the first 20 pilot families and track landlord responses. Publish a plain-language Succession Readiness Score for tenants.

title: Facility-Clearance-in-a-Box and Cleared Bench
one_liner: A facility-clearance sponsor plus a rentable bench of already-cleared engineers for the wave of newly funded defense startups winning first classified subcontracts.
customer: Series A-C defense startups and small business subcontractors with a first classified task order but no facility clearance or cleared staff.
problem: Defense startups raised $14.6B in five months of 2026, and awards are accelerating. Startups cannot sponsor clearances without a contract and cannot start work without cleared people. Sponsorship and adjudication take months, so classified work stalls and startups lose the window.
solution: A cleared small business holds the FCL and employs a bench of cleared engineers, program managers and security officers. It subcontracts them to startups by the hour, provides FSO services, and manages the startup's own path to clearance. Includes shared SCIF time at partner facilities.
why_now: Record capital plus fast-lane vehicles (Megatron IDIQ, the Space Force valley-of-death office, Navy marketplaces) create hundreds of first-time classified subcontractors at once. Federal staff shortages mean primes want ready capacity.
revenue_model: Cleared-labor margin (25-40% on $150-250 per hour), monthly FSO retainers ($4-10K), and SCIF seat fees. A roll-up of small cleared staffing shops adds scale.
non_obvious_insight: Cash is no longer scarce for defense startups, but time-to-cleared-work is. The binding constraint has moved from funding to a slow, government-controlled credential that can be rented.
first_30_days: Acquire or partner with a small cleared firm that already holds an FCL. Recruit 5-8 cleared freelancers and retired government staff. Pitch the 20 most recently funded startups and place the first two engineers.

title: Resin Swap Bureau for Shortage-Hit Molders
one_liner: Fast material-equivalency testing and paperwork for injection molders who must switch resin grades when supply breaks.
customer: Small and mid-size injection molders and extruders with 10-200 employees, and their OEM quality engineers (appliance, auto, medical, electrical).
problem: Hormuz transits run about 10 a day against a baseline of 88-130, and the Gulf is a large polymer and petrochemical exporter (my inference on resin exposure). ISM comments cite long lead times and price volatility. Molders forced to change resin need to requalify with UL recognition, food-contact letters, PPAP and customer sign-off, and testing labs take weeks.
solution: An equivalency database (datasheet parsing plus coupon results) and a fast-turn lab partner. For each part spec it ranks substitutes, runs a five-day test protocol (tensile, impact, heat deflection, melt flow, shrinkage, UL 94 screen, color), and produces the change package: process change notice, PPAP delta and customer approval draft. It tracks UL, FDA and REACH status.
why_now: The war shock and volatility force substitutions now, and lead times are stretching. Molders have no in-house materials engineers.
revenue_model: $2.5-8k per part-family qualification. About $6k a year for database and alerts. Margin on lab work.
non_obvious_insight: In a shortage, finding a substitute resin is easy because a distributor can suggest one. The bottleneck is proving to a customer's QA that the substitute is allowed. The valuable product is the paperwork.
first_30_days: Partner with a certified test lab. Sign five molders. Build the first 50 equivalency sets in one resin family (PP, ABS or PC) from public datasheets. Publish a free shortage swap guide to gather leads.

title: Neutral Caninization Platform for Pet Antibody Drugs
one_liner: A species-adaptation and developability service that lets animal-health companies without Zoetis's proprietary platform make dog, cat and horse antibody drugs.
customer: Mid-size animal-health companies (Elanco, Boehringer Ingelheim Animal Health, Merck Animal Health, Dechra, Ceva, Virbac, Asian vet-pharma) and pet-biotech startups.
problem: Companion-animal mAbs (Cytopoint, Librela, Solensia, Lenivia, Portela) are dominated by one player with roughly 85-90% of revenue, built on a proprietary caninization platform. Others cannot reliably turn a validated human target into a dog- or cat-ready antibody with proper Fc biology, FcRn-driven half-life and low anti-drug-antibody risk. AI binder-design tools are trained on human and mouse data, not canine or feline.
solution: Offer (1) canine, feline and equine germline-framework and Fc libraries with species-specific FcRn and FcgR binding assays, (2) AI-assisted binder design and caninization against validated pet targets (IL-31, NGF, IL-4/13, CD20, PD-1), (3) canine PBMC and ADA-risk screens, and (4) a lead plus data package for USDA or FDA-CVM pathways. Sell as fixed-price programs.
why_now: 2026 review literature names species adaptation and Fc biology as the missing platform pieces. Zero-shot AI antibody design has reached double-digit hit rates, so making binders is cheap while species adaptation is the moat. Zoetis's pet-mAb franchise proves the commercial size, and FDA's expanded conditional approval for major species (through 2028) is available.
revenue_model: $150-400k per program plus milestones and deliberately light royalties, and reagent sales (species-specific FcRn and receptor kits).
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume AI-designed drugs must prove themselves in human oncology. Animal health has smaller and faster trials, direct-pay owners and a concentrated incumbent whose moat is the platform, not the targets. AI attacks exactly that platform. The first AI-designed antibody drug on the market may well be for dogs.
first_30_days: Build canine and feline framework and Fc reagent sets from public sequences and gene synthesis (~$20k). Run FcRn binding on 10 published veterinary mAbs to show calibration. Pitch 15 animal-health BD leads and 5 pet-biotech startups. Sign 1-2 paid feasibility studies ($30-60k), such as caninizing a validated human target.

title: Settlement Passports for Florida High-Rise Condos
one_liner: A satellite-radar settlement history for every Florida condo tower, sold as the cheap first page of the milestone-inspection and reserve-study file.
customer: Florida condo associations and the licensed engineers and property managers who run their milestone inspections and structural integrity reserve studies; secondary buyers are master-policy underwriters, lenders and buyers' agents doing condo diligence.
problem: Carriers want structural documents before they bind a master policy, SIRS and milestone inspections are mandatory for 3+ story buildings, and special assessments run $50K-$200K+ per unit. Boards cannot tell whether their building is stable or sinking until an engineer bills for scoping. A 2024 University of Miami InSAR study found 35 Miami Beach to Sunny Isles buildings subsiding 2-8 cm over 2016-2023, and no commercial product packages this for boards.
solution: Process free Sentinel-1 radar (2015 onward), ESA archive radar for the 1990s-2010s, and newly public NISAR L-band data into a per-building vertical-motion trend. Add differential tilt across the footprint and a comparison against neighbours built on similar fill. Deliver a 3-page Settlement Passport plus a monitoring feed, positioned as a screening indicator that sharpens inspection scope, with an engineer partner signing off. It is not a substitute for the inspection.
why_now: Florida's post-Surfside SB 4-D inspection and reserve-study mandates are now enforced and carriers demand documents. NISAR L-band data has been free through ASF since the July 20, 2026 public release, adding to the Sentinel-1 record. Peer-reviewed proof that InSAR resolves individual Miami towers exists but has not been productized. Reinsurance is softening while condo retail insurance is still squeezed.
revenue_model: $900-$2,500 per building for the initial passport and $300/yr for monitoring. Wholesale price of about $400 to engineering firms who bundle it into SIRS work. $100/building/yr portfolio contracts for management companies.
non_obvious_insight: InSAR is treated as an academic or pipeline-monitoring tool, but the buyer with a legal deadline and a real budget is a condo board that must assemble a structural file. Persistent-scatterer InSAR works best on concrete high-rises, the exact asset at issue. The 10-30 year archive can also show a building has been stable for decades, which makes it a positive underwriting asset for the many buildings that are fine, not just a warning label.
first_30_days: Run the free Sentinel-1 stack for about 400 buildings on the Miami-Dade and Broward barrier islands. Offer one free passport to each of 15 engineering firms and 5 management companies, and sign 2 engineers as resellers. Then charge the first 10 boards facing reserve-study or insurance-renewal deadlines.

title: Owner-Download: Capture Tacit Knowledge Before Sale
one_liner: Passively capture 60-90 days of an owner's calls, messages and jobs into a transferable playbook and a question-answering agent for the buyer.
customer: Owners aged 58+ of owner-dependent service and professional businesses ($300k-3M revenue) planning a sale in 12-36 months, plus the brokers who list them and the buyers who acquire them.
problem: Buyers discount hard for key-person dependency. The knowledge sits in the owner's head and phone: pricing instincts, customer quirks, vendor favors, unwritten rules. The traditional six-month handover rarely captures it.
solution: With consent, capture call recordings, texts and email, invoices, calendar and short weekly AI interviews. Produce SOPs, customer memory cards, learned pricing and quote logic, vendor scorecards and 'if X breaks, do Y' runbooks. The buyer gets a Q&A agent for year one ('how did the owner price gutters over 40 feet?') and the package goes in the data room as a transferable asset.
why_now: Long-context models, cheap call transcription and agentic retrieval make passive capture practical. Loosened SBA financing (up to $10M combined from July 2026) is drawing more first-time buyers who need this.
revenue_model: $2,500-6,000 per owner, broker referral fees, and a $199/month buyer subscription to the Q&A agent for 12 months.
non_obvious_insight: AI did not make this possible by automating the work but by making capture passive, so an owner no longer has to stop working to write manuals. Key-person discount is measurable, so the package can be priced against it.
first_30_days: Recruit five owners through two brokers in one vertical (HVAC, plumbing or landscaping). Run the capture pilots and ask buyers to rate the packages against a control listing on confidence and price.

title: Turnkey Six-Bed Care Homes for Nurse-Operators
one_liner: A licensing-and-operations platform that turns ordinary houses into small licensed residential care homes run by nurses and experienced aides.
customer: Nurses, CNAs and senior aides (including immigrant health workers) who want to own and run a home, plus small investors and families who own a suitable house.
problem: Insiders think the senior-housing gap ($275B, about 549k units by 2028) needs towers, REIT capital and 3-5 year development. Yet many states license 4-10 bed homes in normal single-family zoning. The barriers are licensing know-how, fire and ADA retrofits, staffing plans and a steady flow of admissions, not capital.
solution: A 90-day licensing sprint: zoning and state licensing packet, retrofit checklist, insurance, policies and procedures. Then staffing playbooks (1:3 to 1:6 ratios), charting, medication and compliance software, an admissions pipeline from hospital discharge planners who can't find beds, and financing partners (HELOC, sale-leaseback, small-investor pools). Start with states that have small-home license categories (for example Washington adult family homes, Arizona assisted-living homes and California small RCFEs).
why_now: Occupancy is at 90.1%, the highest since 2007. Inventory growth was 0.4% in Q1 2026, the lowest on record, and nothing new arrives before 2030. Hospital discharge teams are desperate for beds, and seniors hold a record $14.92T in home equity.
revenue_model: $6-12k onboarding fee per home, 5-8% management or software fee on revenue, and a placement fee from families where permitted. Later a captive group-purchasing and insurance program.
non_obvious_insight: Supply can appear in 6 months if the constraint is permission and playbooks, not concrete. One nurse-operator with a 5-bedroom house at $5-7k per resident per month can rival a mid-size facility's per-bed economics with no construction.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 prospective operators through nursing-school and CNA Facebook groups. Sell a $2,500 feasibility-and-licensing sprint, publish a 'how to license a six-bed home in [state]' guide as lead-gen, and line up one hospital discharge planner as a first referral source.

title: Substitute-Plan Binders for Retiring Business Owners
one_liner: Retired teachers interview 60+ owner-operators and write a 'sub plan' any stranger could use to run the shop for a week, sold through business brokers.
customer: Owner-operators aged 60+ of $300k-$3M revenue businesses that depend on the owner's head (HVAC and plumbing, vet and dental practices, hardware stores, salons, daycares, landscaping). The channel and co-payer is the business broker, plus SBA lenders, CPAs and estate attorneys. Acquirers such as search-fund and ETA buyers pay later for a 'day-one' version.
problem: About 40% of small business owners are boomers, and roughly 6 million businesses will change hands by 2035. Around 70% of listed small businesses never sell, and about half of owners have no succession plan. Buyers and lenders can't underwrite what lives only in the owner's memory. Owners refuse to write SOPs, but they will talk for hours. Brokers watch listings die at the diligence stage because 'the business is the owner.'
solution: Two half-day interview sessions plus a video walk-through of the shop. Teachers are trained to draw knowledge out of people with questions. The output is a 20-40 page Sub Plan written in the classroom genre. It covers the daily schedule and routines, where the keys and passwords are, the 'kids to watch' (the difficult customer, the vendor who needs a call before noon, the employee who needs praise), emergency procedures, a first-hour and first-week script, and 'what NOT to do.' The org chart is drawn as a seating chart showing who actually influences whom. Then comes the sub test. A stranger runs a 4-hour shift from the binder, and every gap they hit gets fixed. The result becomes a diligence exhibit in the sale memorandum. AI transcription and structuring keep labor cost low, and the human elicitation stays the scarce part.
why_now: Coverage of the 'Great Ownership Transfer' peaked in 2026 (McKinsey, Forbes and others). First-time buyers via SBA 7(a) loans and search funds are flooding the market and underwriting transferability. AI transcription and structuring dropped the cost of capturing tacit knowledge by roughly 10x in the last two years. The oldest boomers turn 80 this year, and estate attorneys are seeing more 'owner died, business worthless in 90 days' cases.
revenue_model: $2,400 flat per binder, usually rolled into the broker's listing package. Brokers get a referral credit of about $300. There is a $49/month 'living binder' update plan. Buyers can pay $1,500 for a post-close rewrite. There is a $600 add-on for estate attorneys covering an 'if I'm hit by a bus' version.
non_obvious_insight: The sub plan is the most battle-tested knowledge-transfer document in existence. Every teacher has written hundreds of them for a stranger with 30 unpredictable kids and six hours. No consultant has that reps count. The real asset in a small business is the informal 'kids to watch' list, which never appears in any SOP. Sellers don't fail because they lack documents. They fail because nobody asked the right questions in the right order.
first_30_days: Recruit 4-5 retired teachers who like interviewing. Pick one metro and pitch 20 business brokers with one offer: 'give me your stalest listing, the one that has sat 9+ months, and I'll run a free pilot binder.' Do 3 free pilots in exchange for testimonials and an intro to the broker's next 5 listings. Then charge $2,400. Add SCORE chapters, SBDCs and estate attorneys as second-wave channels.

title: NOI Haircut Reports for Multifamily Underwriting
one_liner: A 24-hour diligence report that restates a multifamily property's NOI for real concessions, renewal cliffs and banned fee income, sold to the lenders and buyers who will feel it first.
customer: Debt funds, CRE CLO managers, agency-lender underwriting teams and mid-market syndicators buying 100-1,000 unit properties in concession-heavy or fee-regulated markets.
problem: Headline NOI rests on face rents and other income. Concessions run 15.8% of stabilized units and 1.2M units are still in lease-up, and leases signed with free months renew at face rent a year later, inviting churn. Fee income (admin, pet, package, parking) is being banned: Seattle from July 2027 with treble damages, and the NAA tracked 140 fee bills in 2025. Sellers' T-12s show neither risk.
solution: Upload rent roll, T-12 and fee schedule and receive net-effective rent by lease cohort, concession burn-off and renewal-cliff dates, fee income at risk by jurisdiction and effective date, and a stressed NOI and DSCR. A monitoring API flags changes across a loan book as laws pass.
why_now: Concessions are now the pricing lever because rent cuts hurt valuations and algorithmic pricing is legally constrained. Dated fee bans give lenders a hard clock, and the rental supply wave has crested, so underwriting errors will show up in 2027 renewals.
revenue_model: $750-2,500 per report; $2-5K per monitored loan per year; enterprise API licenses to lenders.
non_obvious_insight: NOI has become a policy variable, but underwriting models still treat it as a market variable. The party whose model breaks first is the lender, not the operator, and lenders have diligence budgets.
first_30_days: Build a law and effective-date database for the 10 states and cities with fee rules. Publish three public teardown case studies on listed properties. Sell $500 pilot reports to 10 syndicators via LinkedIn and BiggerPockets, then pitch two debt funds on a diligence add-on.

title: Conformity Cases for Learning-Enabled Robots
one_liner: A compliance workbench and pre-assessment service that builds the CE-marking safety case for machines whose behaviour comes from ML models (warehouse robots, cobots, humanoids) ahead of the new EU Machinery Regulation.
customer: CTOs and safety engineers at robotics startups and integrators (10-300 staff) selling autonomous mobile robots, cobot cells, agri-robots, humanoids and exoskeletons into the EU.
problem: The Machinery Regulation applies from 20 Jan 2027 and adds duties for machinery with self-evolving or learning behaviour and for cybersecurity (background, verify), with AI Act Annex I overlay dated 2 Aug 2028 in the tracker. Consultancies know ISO 12100 and 13849 but not how to argue the safety of a neural-network policy, notified bodies have no playbook, and startups cannot sell to EU customers without a CE dossier.
solution: Software plus an expert network: hazard-analysis templates for ML perception and control, runtime safety-monitor patterns (shielding, safe fallback, speed and separation monitoring), test evidence generated from simulation and field logs, and a traceable assurance case linking hazards to mitigations to evidence, mapped to Machinery, CRA and AI Act. A partner notified body does a pre-review.
why_now: Foundation-model-controlled and humanoid robots reached commercial pilots in 2025-26, and the regulatory dates arrive within months. Assurance-case methods from aviation and automated driving are mature but have not reached robotics.
revenue_model: EUR 25-80k per product safety-case project, $2-6k/month SaaS, and notified-body referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: The blocker for deploying humanoids in Europe is not the model but an argument a regulator can accept. The first team whose safety cases are accepted creates precedent that competitors must copy, which is a durable moat.
first_30_days: Interview 20 robotics startups and publish an 'ML robot CE checklist'. Sign three design partners at EUR 10-15k for a gap analysis and recruit an ex-notified-body functional-safety engineer as co-founder or advisor.

title: A Teaching Hospital Inside a Dead Hospital
one_liner: Lease a wing of a closed hospital and run it as a full-scale simulation hospital that nursing schools rent by the student-day.
customer: Community-college ADN and BSN programs turning away applicants, state workforce boards, and health systems that want a new-grad pipeline.
problem: Nursing schools turned away a record 93,176 qualified applications in 2025 (AACN, May 2026). The binding constraint is clinical placement sites, plus faculty vacancies above 7%. Many state boards allow up to 50% of clinical hours in high-fidelity simulation, but most school sim labs are a few beds in a converted classroom. Medicaid cuts are pushing more rural hospitals to close.
solution: Lease a closed hospital floor that already has medical gas, patient rooms, nurse stations, ICU bays and an OR. Fill it with liquidation beds and mannequins. Staff it with simulation faculty and local standardized patients such as retirees and theater students. Run immersive multi-day, 12-hour shift simulations from admission to discharge, sold per student-day or by semester cohort. Design to NCSBN and INACSL standards and get state board sign-off.
why_now: The record turned-away numbers landed in May 2026. 38 state boards had specific simulation rules by 2021 and more have followed. Rural closures are rising with the 2025 federal Medicaid cuts, so vacant, fully plumbed buildings are appearing cheaply. The $10B/yr Rural Health Transformation funds (FY26-30) create state workforce money to pay for seats.
revenue_model: $150-300 per student-day, or cohort contracts of $40-120k per semester per program. Health-system sponsorship for pipeline seats. Workforce and state grant funding.
non_obvious_insight: Simulation labs fail from unrealistic space and thin faculty, not from a lack of mannequins, and a dead hospital is the only building that already is the environment, priced at less than replacement cost. The buyer is a school with a waitlist, backed by employers and state money that want more graduates.
first_30_days: Pick two states with permissive simulation rules and long nursing waitlists. Call ADN program directors at 10 community colleges and offer a paid 2-day 'shift-in-a-day' pilot. Identify 3 closed hospitals through state health-department lists. Recruit a retired nurse educator as clinical lead, rent mannequins for a pilot, and charge $12-20k per cohort.

title: Notice Desk with Contingency Penalty Abatement
one_liner: Snap a photo of any IRS or state notice, get triage and a response, and pay only if the penalty is abated.
customer: 1-25 employee firms, S-corps and small partnerships that received late-filing, payroll-deposit, information-return mismatch or state tax notices.
problem: Notices sit in a drawer or a registered-agent inbox while penalties compound. Abatement routes (first-time abatement, reasonable cause, small-partnership relief) are well established but owners don't know them, and CPAs bill hourly. Filing rules are shifting: the 1099-NEC floor rose to $2,000, 1099-K thresholds reverted, and new tips and overtime reporting will create mismatches. IRS capacity appears strained (prior knowledge).
solution: Forward or photograph the notice. The system classifies it, extracts the deadline and amount, explains the options and drafts the response. An enrolled agent or CPA partner signs, files the abatement request and tracks it. State-notice variants are added by jurisdiction. A $19/month mail-monitoring plan for registered-agent customers catches new notices.
why_now: BOI filing services just lost their main product and need a new recurring hook, and compliance work is moving from filing to interpretation. LLMs can read notices at scale.
revenue_model: 20% of penalties abated, $49 flat for triage on notices with no abatement path, and $19/month monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: A penalty notice is a lead with a known dollar value. Many abatements are near-automatic, so outcome pricing beats hourly billing, and Intuit, Xero and H&R Block cannot easily price on outcomes.
first_30_days: Get 100 anonymized notices from CPA partners and registered-agent companies to train the classifier. Sign an enrolled agent, run 30 abatements sourced from small-business forums, and record the abatement rate.

title: Vet-Supervised Cattle Crews for the Screwworm Era
one_liner: Custom-harvester-style crews do the 80% of a vet's working day that is labor (inspect, treat navels, tag, record) so the scarce vet supervises and signs instead of holding the chute.
customer: Ranchers in screwworm zones and buffer states (Texas, New Mexico, Oklahoma) paying per head or per day; sale barns, stocker operations and feedlots that need pre-movement inspection documentation; and overloaded rural vet practices that subcontract overflow to a crew.
problem: Only about 1.3% of vets work in food animal practice, and South Texas vets say it will not be physically possible to handle every screwworm case. Daily inspection is the core control, newborn calves' navels are prime targets (past outbreaks saw navel strike rates as high as 50% in unprotected calves), and ranchers with 300-3,000 head across brush country do not have the labor to look at every animal every day.
solution: A vet-supervised service company (a rural vet as medical director, or a vet-owned entity) fielding 3-4 person crews with a trailer: portable squeeze chute, EID reader, wound-care kit, vet-approved treatment protocols, and a photo- and GPS-stamped inspection log that the vet countersigns. The seasonal product is an 'NWS Season Program' of scheduled pasture rounds, navel treatment on newborn calves, wound checks, prescribed prophylactic treatments under an existing VCPR, and movement paperwork. Off-season the same crews run preg-checks, weaning, vaccination and processing days year-round, with the vet doing exams and sign-off.
why_now: The first US screwworm detections came in Texas in June 2026, followed by more counties, a New Mexico detection, and the first infested horse in September. Sterile fly supply is constrained, federal and state agencies have imposed movement restrictions and mandatory veterinary inspections in affected areas, and FDA has moved to authorize treatment products. Spring calving in Texas is the next high-risk window.
revenue_model: $3-8 per head per treatment or round, day rates around $1,800-2,500 per crew for working days, seasonal retainer contracts, and a 20-30% margin on subcontracted overflow from vet practices. Target roughly 35-40% gross margin per crew.
non_obvious_insight: The vet shortage is largely a labor-allocation problem: a $250-per-hour license is spent on tasks that only need hands. Custom crews are normal for harvest, hay and branding, but herd health stayed in-house because vets never delegated it formally. Practice-of-veterinary-medicine laws let a supervising vet delegate many tasks, and once the vet is medical director of record the boundary is workable. The durable asset is the trained crew that keeps earning long after screwworm fades, because labor-short ranches will keep buying it.
first_30_days: Sign 2 overloaded vets in Texas or New Mexico as medical directors, and confirm what each state's practice act allows non-vets to do. Buy a used portable chute, trailer and 2 EID readers (about $15K), recruit 3 experienced ranch hands or vet-tech students, and get liability coverage. Sell 5 ranches a fall program of weaning-time inspections and navel and wound checks on fall-calving herds, then sell the spring calving program from the results.

title: Independent Conformance Bench for CMS-0057-F APIs
one_liner: A testing-and-attestation service that runs the open-source Inferno and Da Vinci test kits against a health plan's real FHIR APIs and produces the evidence pack its compliance officer needs before January 2027.
customer: Small and mid-size Medicaid managed-care plans, regional Medicare Advantage plans, CHIP managed-care entities, TPAs and the small payer-IT vendors serving them. Buyer is the compliance officer or CIO who signed a vendor contract and can't verify it.
problem: CMS-0057-F requires four FHIR APIs (Patient Access, Provider Access, Payer-to-Payer, Prior Authorization) by 1 Jan 2027, and the 72-hour and 7-day decision timelines have applied since Jan 2026. Plans bought vendor stacks and hear 'we're compliant,' but the plan carries the liability. CMS points at ONC's Inferno tooling, yet almost no one independent runs it against the plan's production-like environment and writes the attestation.
solution: A managed test bench: Inferno with the Da Vinci PAS/CRD/DTR and CARIN test kits, Synthea synthetic members mapped to the plan's data model, latency and load tests aligned to the decision-time metrics, and SMART/OAuth security checks. Deliverables are a pass/fail matrix, remediation tickets for the vendor, an executive attestation binder, and quarterly regression runs as vendors ship updates.
why_now: Guidance is that plans commit to a stack by Q3 2026 to leave time for testing, so Q4 2026 is the test window. It is late September. The rule is fixed, the open-source test kits exist, and the buyers' vendors have a conflict of interest in grading themselves.
revenue_model: Fixed-fee readiness assessment of USD 15-40k. Quarterly regression subscription of USD 3-8k per month. Vendor-side 'independently tested' certification fee. Optional remediation project work.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer isn't engineering; it's a compliance officer who needs independent evidence to hold a vendor to account. Inferno has huge adoption among developers but has never been packaged as an auditor's deliverable. Independence, not tooling, is the product.
first_30_days: Spin up a hosted Inferno plus Synthea environment. Publish a free 'CMS-0057-F self-test cheat sheet.' Approach 10 Medicaid MCO compliance officers through state Medicaid association events and LinkedIn. Sell three pilot assessments at about USD 10k to build case studies before year-end. Partner with FHIR consultancies that lack independent status.

title: Outfall Guardian for Data-Center Construction Sites
one_liner: Continuous outfall monitoring, rapid pathogen testing and auto-generated permit paperwork for contractors building data-center campuses and fabs.
customer: General contractors, owner's representatives and developers building $1B+ data-center and semiconductor campuses. Multi-million-dollar schedule risk gives them a real budget, and the contractor or owner pays.
problem: Cheyenne revoked Meta's discharge permit after a rare bacterium in its wastewater was traced to a construction site, and Ohio scrapped a general permit after more than 7,000 comments. Water quality, not just quantity, is now a siting risk. Contractors treat water as volume and have no biology or continuous-monitoring capability during dewatering, stormwater and hydrostatic testing.
solution: Off-the-shelf multiparameter sensors (turbidity, pH, conductivity, temperature) at each outfall, weekly rapid qPCR pathogen and bacterial testing through a partner lab, automated discharge-monitoring reports and a time-stamped 'permit defense file' that shows compliance before regulators ask. Add a community-facing dashboard.
why_now: Moratoria, permit revocations and public comment fights make regulators and neighbors ask for data. Capex on campuses has exploded, and delay costs are large.
revenue_model: $3-8k/site/month plus per-test lab fees and onboarding fees.
non_obvious_insight: The construction phase is the unmonitored weak link in a water-quality chain everyone else audits. Third-party telemetry works like insurance-grade evidence, and the buyer's motive is schedule protection, not sustainability.
first_30_days: Publish an analysis of the Cheyenne case as top-of-funnel. Contact 10 contractors and owner's reps active in Northern Virginia, Ohio, Texas, Wyoming and Arizona. Pilot at one site with commercial sensors and a contract lab, and offer the first month free in exchange for a case study.

title: School Deepfake-Nude Incident Response Retainer
one_liner: A 24/7 retainer that walks school districts through the first 72 hours of an AI-generated nude incident: hash-based takedowns, evidence handling, reporting duties and parent communications.
customer: School districts, charter networks and independent schools. Channel: school risk pools, cyber and liability insurers and brokers.
problem: Nudify apps let anyone turn a student photo into sexual imagery. Schools improvise: staff viewing the images can itself be illegal, mandated-reporting and Title IX duties are unclear, and takedowns must be filed on many platforms. The federal TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025) requires platforms to remove reported intimate imagery within 48 hours, with platform compliance due May 2026 (from memory), but victims and schools don't know the process.
solution: A playbook plus tooling: secure intake that hashes images without staff viewing them (StopNCII and NCMEC Take It Down style), pre-filled takedown requests, a state-by-state legal duty checklist, evidence logs, communication templates for parents and students, and counselor referral. A retained hotline handles live incidents.
why_now: The TAKE IT DOWN Act's platform obligations kicked in this year, incidents are proliferating, and insurers are re-underwriting districts for cyber and child-safety exposure.
revenue_model: $3-12k annual retainer per district, per-incident fees, and bundle or referral deals with insurers and school risk pools.
non_obvious_insight: The worst thing a school can do is look at the evidence, so the product is a don't-look-just-hash workflow. Insurers are the channel because one mishandled incident costs far more than the retainer.
first_30_days: Draft the playbook with a school-law attorney and a former juvenile detective. Pitch 3 school-insurance brokers or state school-board risk pools. Run free tabletop exercises for 5 districts. Convert the best relationship into the first paid retainer.
